analysis.one_liner: Requires oil and gas fracking sites to test nearby drinking water for contamination and report results publicly.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote; it died in the House Energy and Commerce Committee with 38 Democratic sponsors and cosponsors and no Republican support.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would require companies that frack for oil, gas, or geothermal energy to test underground drinking water near their wells for contamination, repeat the testing every six months during operations and annually for five years after, and report the results within two weeks. The Environmental Protection Agency would have to post all results in a public, ZIP-Code-searchable database, so residents could look up what was found near their homes. States that want authority over underground injection programs would have to adopt the same testing rule for their fracking operations.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live near fracking sites, especially households that rely on well water. They would get regular testing of nearby drinking water and a public database they could search by ZIP Code to see whether contamination was found. The testing would happen before drilling starts, every six months during operations, and annually for five years afterward.

how_it_helps.text: The bill requires fracking operators to test all accessible underground drinking water sources within a half mile of a well site — or the nearest one within a mile — before injection starts, every six months during operations, and at least annually for five years after operations end.

Operators must report the results to the EPA within two weeks of each test, and the EPA must maintain a publicly accessible, searchable database of the results, searchable by ZIP Code, so members of the public can easily identify sites near them.
Testing must be done by EPA-certified laboratories and cover any hazardous substance or contaminant that the EPA determines would indicate fracking-related damage.

States seeking primary enforcement responsibility for underground injection control programs must prohibit fracking injection unless operators agree to the testing and reporting requirements, extending the rule nationwide through state programs.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies that frack. They would pay for regular laboratory testing of water sources within a half mile of each site, reporting, and — if contamination were found — the exposure that comes with documented evidence of it. Sites with no accessible drinking water within one mile are exempt, which limits who pays.

drawbacks.text: The bill creates no penalty or remedy beyond testing and reporting: it documents contamination but does not directly stop it, clean it up, or pay residents whose water is damaged.

Sites with no accessible underground drinking water within a one-mile radius are entirely exempt, and the definition of 'accessible' turns on whether the operator can reasonably gain access to the water source — leaving some vulnerable aquifers untested.
Operators would bear recurring testing and reporting costs on every active well, a cost that small operators may pass on or that could reduce drilling in some areas.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is concrete: residents near fracking sites would get regularly tested drinking water and a searchable public record of the results, which today they largely do not have. The cost falls on fracking operators, and the main weaknesses are that the bill detects contamination without providing a remedy, and its exemptions leave some water sources untested. On balance it is a modest transparency measure rather than a ban or a cleanup program.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Environment and Climate Change subcommittee, which never took it up, so it died when the 117th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Janice Schakowsky introduced the bill on March 23, 2021, joined by 37 Democratic cosponsors; no Republicans cosponsored it.
The House referred it to the Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day, and the next day it went to the Subcommittee on Environment and Climate Change.
No hearing, markup, or vote ever followed; the bill never left the subcommittee and expired with the 117th Congress on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas fracking operators, who avoided new testing, reporting, and public-disclosure obligations; residents near drilling sites got no new information about their water.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fracking operators avoided new testing duties

sides.party_line_note: All 38 sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats and no Republican signed on; the House never reached a roll call, so no vote breakdown exists.

industries.note: The bill would impose recurring testing, reporting, and public disclosure on every well site within a mile of drinking water, and documented contamination would create liability exposure. Avoiding that testing is the industry's interest, which runs against residents' interest in knowing whether their water is safe.
All required testing must be done by certified laboratories, so the bill would create a large stream of paid testing work. This aligns with the bill's purpose of producing water-quality data.

The bill covers fracking used for geothermal production too, so geothermal operators would face the same testing and reporting duties. Their compliance burden matches the public benefit of disclosure.
